studies.title: Even His Fingertips
studies.meaning: Two oaths open the surah, both carrying a negative particle the grammarians have long discussed, and then comes the question they were preparing for. The objection assumed is about bones, which was the Meccan form of the argument. The answer deliberately overshoots it: not the bones but the fingertips, the smallest and most individuated thing a body has. The final line then moves the dispute somewhere else entirely. The problem is not treated as an error in reasoning but as a wish about what lies ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The Meccan dispute about resurrection was concrete and physical, turning on scattered and decayed remains rather than on God's existence, and several early surahs answer it in exactly those terms. This chapter is given over almost entirely to the subject. No specific occasion is reported for its opening, which is framed as a general statement about the human being rather than about anyone named.

keyTerms.note: The word names the ends of the fingers. The Quran uses it twice in all, and the other occurrence is a description of battle, which makes this the only place it appears as a detail of the body's design.
The verb means bringing a thing into proportion. It is used elsewhere of forming the human being and of the sky being levelled, so fingertips are described with the vocabulary of large construction.

From a root for splitting open, which also gives the word for daybreak. It names breaking past a boundary, so the objection is described as wanting the road ahead left open rather than as a conclusion reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burial in Arabia was shallow and the desert did the rest. People had seen old graves opened by wind and by animals, and bones lying bleached near an abandoned camp were an ordinary sight on any long journey. The Meccan objection was not abstract philosophy. It came from men who could point at what was left of somebody they had known and ask the question standing over it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for fingertips occurs twice in the Quran, and the two uses could hardly be further apart. Here it marks the finest detail of the body's assembly, offered as the outer limit of what reassembly might include. In the other place it appears in the middle of a battle scene, naming the part of an enemy to strike.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer works by raising the bid rather than by arguing. The objector chose the hardest case he could think of, and the reply moves past it to something harder still, which is a way of saying the difficulty was never located where he put it. And the last line changes the subject from capacity to motive, so the passage ends by describing denial as something a person wants rather than something he has worked out.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same objection, put by a man holding a decayed bone in his hand.
Records the objection in its Meccan wording: when we are bones and fragments.
Says God knows what the earth takes away of them, and keeps a record that holds.

studies.applyIt: Look at your own fingertip for a moment. The pattern on it belongs to nobody else alive, and you had no part in arranging it. This passage reaches past every larger argument to pick out that one detail. Whatever you make of the rest, give ten seconds to the evidence it actually names.

studies.title: Where Is The Escape
studies.meaning: The question is asked in a tone the passage treats as a challenge rather than an enquiry, and it gets three physical events instead of a date. Sight fails, the moon goes dark, and the two great lights are gathered together, which commentators read as the sun and moon losing their separation and taking the whole apparatus of time with them. The answer ends with the questioner's own voice returning, now asking something different. The second question belongs to the same man, and it is not answered either.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. Demands for a date were a standing feature of the Meccan objection, and the Quran meets them in several places by describing the event and refusing the timing. The two lights here are not decoration. This was a society that navigated, traded and dated everything by them, so losing both at once is the loss of the framework rather than of the scenery.

keyTerms.note: From the root for lightning. It names the state of an eye that has taken a flash: open, fixed, and seeing nothing at all, which is not blindness but an excess of light.
The verb used of ground giving way and taking down whatever stood on it. Applied to the moon it says the light was not covered over but drawn under, which is a different picture from an eclipse.
A noun of place from the verb to flee. The definite article turns it into a specific location, so the question assumes such a place exists somewhere and only asks for directions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sun set the working day and the moon set the calendar, the markets, the debts and the pilgrimage months. A merchant's contract fell due by a moon and a caravan's departure was fixed by a season the sun determined. Losing either would have upended ordinary life in the valley. This passage removes both at once, and with them every instrument the audience had for saying when anything was.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used of the moon here is the same one the Quran uses for the earth opening and swallowing a man together with his house. Arabic treats an eclipse as a sinking rather than a covering, so the image is of the moon being taken down rather than hidden, which is not the picture the English word carries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to supply a date is consistent across the Quran, and the substitution here is instructive. Instead of when, the answer describes what it will be like from the inside. That moves the question off the calendar and onto the person asking. And the closing line hands the questioner a second question, which shows the first one being answered by experience rather than by information.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand for a date and returns the same refusal, in the same register.
Opens with the sun wound up and the stars falling, dismantling the sky the same way.
Shows a man offering everyone he has in exchange for an escape on that Day.

studies.applyIt: The second question in this passage is the more honest one. Notice, this week, the moment a question of yours shifts from wanting information to wanting a way out. From the inside they sound identical. The difference is whether you would accept an answer that happened not to help you.

studies.title: Evidence Against Himself
studies.meaning: The question just asked is cut off rather than answered, and the reply removes its premise: there is no such place. What follows is a sequence. The settling is with your Lord; the record is read out in both directions, forward and back; and then the man himself becomes the evidence. The last clause is the sharpest. He goes on producing excuses while being the proof against himself, and the two happen at once rather than in turn. The word for evidence can also mean insight, and commentators take both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, inside a surah given over to resurrection. The vocabulary here is borrowed from a procedure the audience knew well: a settlement, a notification, a witness and a defence. Disputes were taken to an arbiter, claims were stated in front of everybody, and a man's witnesses were his real strength. The passage takes that apparatus intact and removes the possibility of a friendly witness.

keyTerms.note: The word originally names the mountain fastness a man retreats into. The same root gives the word for a burden carried on the back, so the place of safety and the weight share an origin.
A noun of place from the verb to come to rest. It names both where a thing finally stops moving and where a case is finally resolved, and both senses are working here at once.
An intensive form from the verb to see. It means both the faculty of insight and a piece of plain evidence, and that double sense is why the ayah reads as a man and his own seeing being one witness.

A plural from the root for excusing, occurring once in the Quran. Some early readers took it from a different root, as the curtains a man lets down to screen himself, which would make it concealment rather than speech.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was public and built on witnesses. A man who could produce respected men to speak for him could carry a case; a man who could not was finished before he opened his mouth, whatever the facts happened to be. Everybody knew how to assemble that support in advance, and the strength of a claim was often the strength of the names behind it. Here the only witness in the room is the defendant.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the excuses in the last of these ayat occurs once in the Quran, and the early readers were divided about what it even means. One reading takes it as the plural of an excuse offered aloud. Another traces it to a different root entirely, as the coverings a man drops to hide behind. Both are recorded, and neither was set aside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes every mechanism people use to manage a verdict. There is nowhere to go, no stage at which the record gets negotiated, and no witness to arrange in advance. What is left is a man and his own clear sight, which is a more uncomfortable arrangement than an external judge would be. And naming what he left behind widens the account past his actions to the consequences that outlived him.

crossReferences.why: Has the hands speak and the feet testify while the mouths themselves are sealed.
Tells a man to read his own record: today you are sufficient as your own reckoner.
Describes hearing, sight and skin testifying against the person they belonged to.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing you did this week and the excuse you gave for it, two lines, one under the other. Do not argue with either line. Most excuses survive because they are never set next to the thing they explain. This passage claims that you already know which of the two is true.

studies.title: Do Not Hurry Your Tongue
studies.meaning: The surah breaks off its subject for four ayat and addresses the man receiving it. He has been moving his tongue along with the revelation as it arrives, trying to fix it before it can slip, and he is told to stop. Three things are then assigned away from him: the gathering of it, the reciting of it, and afterwards the explaining of it. One instruction is left with him, which is to follow. The aside is preserved in the text, so a reader gets both the anxiety and the answer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The classical accounts describe the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) repeating the words as they came, out of fear of losing any part of them, and read this passage as addressing that habit directly. The surah then resumes its subject in the very next ayah as though nothing had interrupted. Why the aside sits inside a chapter on resurrection is not explained by the commentators.

keyTerms.gloss: do not move, do not stir
keyTerms.note: A plain verb of movement applied to the tongue. The instruction is physical rather than mental: not stop worrying about it, but stop the motion you are making while you listen.

The verbal noun of assembling scattered things. It shares its root with the word used fourteen ayat earlier for bones being reassembled, putting the keeping of a revelation and the raising of a body into one vocabulary.
From a root for separating and making distinct. It names drawing out what a thing means, and assigning it here leaves interpretation as something given rather than something achieved by effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nothing was written down casually. Poetry, genealogy and the terms of treaties were carried in memory by men trained to hold them, and a reciter who lost a line had lost it permanently. The anxiety described here is the entirely reasonable anxiety of somebody in an oral culture receiving something he cannot afford to drop. The instruction runs against every instinct that culture spent generations training.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for gathering the revelation shares its root with the word used fourteen ayat earlier for reassembling a man's scattered bones. The surah is about bodies being collected after they have come apart, and in the middle of it the same verb is turned on a recitation being held together. One root serves both operations.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility for the text is assigned away from the person carrying it, in three separate clauses, which makes preservation a divine act rather than a human achievement. What remains with him is following, and even the meaning is promised afterwards rather than assumed. That sets a pattern for every later reader as well: understanding arrives second, and the first move is to receive without rushing it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in other words: do not hurry with the recitation before it is finished.
Promises directly that he will be made to recite and will not forget what he is given.
Explains the staged sending as a way of steadying the heart and supplying explanations.

studies.applyIt: Notice what the instruction actually is: stop moving your tongue. Next time you read the Quran, read three ayat and then sit with them for the length of one slow breath before going on. The passage treats hurry as the obstacle, and the man it addressed was hurrying for the best reason anybody has ever had.

studies.title: Two Kinds Of Faces
studies.meaning: Two sets of faces, each given two lines, and the symmetry is exact. The first is fresh and turned toward their Lord; the second is scowling and expecting something that breaks the back. The two words used of the first set differ by a single letter and sound almost identical, one meaning in bloom and the other meaning looking, so the Arabic makes radiance and gaze into a near-rhyme. The classical tradition has read the second of them in more than one way and records the readings side by side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, and the line immediately before is still addressing the audience directly, for loving what is immediate and letting the later thing go. The surah then turns to the Day itself. Describing outcomes by faces rather than by names or deeds recurs across the earliest surahs, spoken to a society that read faces closely and did most of its reading in public.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of plants after rain and of a face in good condition. It means bloom rather than shine, so the picture is health returning to something rather than light being added to it.

It differs from the preceding word by one letter and sounds nearly the same. Arabic sets the pair together deliberately here, and the classical readings of what the looking means are recorded without being resolved.
From the same root as one of the two verbs used earlier in the Quran for a man's face closing against the recitation. The identical expression turns up again, now worn on the far side of the event.
Named from the vertebrae. Arabic calls a catastrophe by the bone it snaps, which keeps the abstraction physical, and the word occurs once in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A face was public information. Meetings happened without privacy, news arrived in front of everybody present, and a man's expression when he heard it was witnessed and repeated afterwards. Poets described faces in close detail because their audiences read them for a living. Describing an entire Day by two expressions was therefore not a poetic flourish. It was the most direct report available in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words describing the first set of faces differ by one letter and rhyme with each other, and the word for the second set comes from the same root as a verb the Quran uses earlier for a man's face closing in refusal. The same expression appears twice in the Book: once as something chosen in this life, once as a condition on that Day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Outcomes are described entirely by faces, which keeps both the reward and the loss relational rather than material. Nothing is said about what either group receives. The first set is described by where it is looking and the second by what it is anticipating, so both states are constituted by an orientation rather than by a possession. What is at stake turns out to be attention, which is exactly what the preceding ayah accused the audience of misdirecting.

crossReferences.why: Divides the same Day by faces: bright and laughing against faces covered in dust.
Promises the best and more besides, with no dust and no humiliation on their faces.
Describes faces whitening and faces darkening on the Day as the whole of the account.

studies.applyIt: Think about what your face does when you get news you did not want. This passage divides everything by that one thing. Today, catch your own expression once in the middle of an ordinary irritation, and simply notice it without correcting it. It is a more honest record than anything you would say about yourself out loud.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: When It Reaches The Collarbones
studies.meaning: The scene is a deathbed, reported from the edges rather than from inside it. Something reaches the collarbones and the passage never says what. Somebody in the room asks who can cure him, which commentators read as the people present or as the angels. Then the man himself knows what is happening. The last two ayat are famously disputed: the shins wound together has been read as the body's own legs, as one affliction folding into another, and as this world and the next meeting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah has argued about resurrection and described the Day, and now comes back to the one moment its audience could neither deny nor postpone. Deathbeds in Mecca were crowded and public, with family and neighbours in the room. The passage reports what those people had witnessed many times over, and it stops at precisely the point where their knowledge stops.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a specific bone at the base of the throat. Naming it fixes the moment exactly, since the soul reaching this point was the ordinary Arabic expression for the last instant of a life.
From a root covering both ascending and reciting over a sick person. The question therefore carries both senses at once, and the ambiguity between the two is recorded as old.
A noun from the verb used of driving livestock along a road. It closes the passage with the image of being moved rather than travelling, which is a passive word to end a life on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dying happened at home with the room full. There were no professionals to send for beyond somebody who knew remedies or who would recite over the sick, and the question in the second of these ayat is the question people actually asked out loud. Everyone present had seen the sequence before and knew the signs, and knew too that past a certain point nobody in the room could do anything except stay.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the collarbones occurs once in the Quran, and the phrase it belongs to was already an everyday Arabic expression for the final moment, used the way English speaks of drawing a last breath. The Quran takes a common idiom about dying and makes it anatomically exact by naming the bone the phrase turns on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to describe the thing itself. Something rises, a question is asked and not answered, and the last word is about being driven somewhere. That reticence is deliberate: death is shown from the outside because outside is where every living reader is standing. And the destination is named as a Lord rather than as a place, which makes the end of a life an arrival rather than a stop.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same moment from the same vantage: the soul at the throat, onlookers unable to see.
Shows the angels present at the moment of death with their hands stretched out.
Names the stupor of death arriving with the very thing a person had been avoiding.

studies.applyIt: Sit with somebody who is ill this week, even briefly, and do not try to fix anything. The question this passage asks is who can cure him, and it goes unanswered in the room. Being there is the part that is actually available. Most people leave because they have nothing to offer, which has it exactly backwards.

studies.title: He Went Home Swaggering
studies.meaning: Four negative verbs and then one positive one, and the positive one is a walk. Everything before it is refusal; what he actually does is go home stretching himself out with pleasure. Lexicographers connect that verb to the word for the back, so the picture is a body lengthening its own stride. The passage closes on a phrase repeated twice which the grammarians treat as a threat with its content deliberately withheld, and that is the surah's last word on him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The classical accounts attach the picture to a leading Meccan leaving a gathering where he had heard the recitation, though the reports differ over who is meant and treat the portrait as the thing that matters. Going home to your household after a public encounter and giving your version of it was how opinion in a small town actually formed and hardened.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truthfulness. The verb is not simply to believe but to confirm somebody's report as true, which makes the refusal a judgement passed on a speaker rather than only on a claim.
A reflexive verb for stretching yourself as you move. Lexicographers connect it to the word for the back, so the image is a man drawing out his own stride. It occurs once in the Quran.

keyTerms.gloss: nearer to you, fitter for you
keyTerms.note: An elative meaning closer or more deserving, standing with no noun after it. The threat works by leaving its object unstated, so what is nearer is never named and the repetition does the rest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: How a man walked was read and recorded. Poetry describes gaits in detail, and a deliberately extended stride was a recognised display of standing, the physical form of a boast. Walking that way through a small town where everybody knew your father's name was a statement made to be witnessed, not a private pleasure. The Quran elsewhere instructs believers against it, which shows how legible the gesture was.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the man's walk occurs once in the whole Quran. Lexicographers derive it from the word for the back, so the picture is not speed and not quite strutting but a body drawn out to its full length in satisfaction. One word carries an entire posture, and it is placed at the end of a list of things the man failed to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence puts the interior and the exterior in order and shows them matching. Four refusals, and then a body visibly pleased with itself. The passage is not charging him with arrogance as a separate fault; it is showing what refusal looks like from outside once it has got home and relaxed. The unstated threat that closes it leaves the consequence undescribed, in a surah that has already described a great deal.

crossReferences.why: Instructs against walking the earth in exultation, naming this same display directly.
Says you will not split the earth nor reach the mountains in height by walking so.
Shows a man calling the revelation old tales, with rust settled over his heart.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you leave a conversation you have won. There is a particular lightness to walking away from a disagreement satisfied with yourself, and it is physical before it is anything else. Catch it once this week. This passage does not describe the man's thoughts at all. It describes his walk.

studies.title: Left Loose With No Owner
studies.meaning: One question opens the passage and another closes it, and the material in between is a short biography running backwards to its start. Left with no purpose, unattended, is what the word suggests, and the classical readers gloss it as an animal turned loose with nobody responsible for it. Then three stages of formation, ending with the division into two sexes. The final question is rhetorical and small: could the one who did that not do it again.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah entirely about the Day of Resurrection, which it opens by swearing by. The ayat just before describe a man walking home to his family full of self-satisfaction. No specific occasion is reported. The Meccan objection the surah answers throughout was not about God but about whether scattered bones could be reassembled, and this passage answers it from embryology rather than from power.

keyTerms.note: Used of a camel left to wander with no herdsman and no purpose assigned to it. The word covers both being unsupervised and being pointless, which is why the question lands on two things at once.
A verb of levelling and balancing, used of smoothing a surface. Applied to a body it names the arrangement of parts in proportion, which is a separate act from bringing them into existence.
From a root meaning to hang or cling, the same root behind the word for a leech. It names the stage by its behaviour, attachment, rather than by its appearance or its size.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals were the measure of everything in Arabia, and a camel left loose with no owner was a recognised category: unbranded, unattended, and belonging to nobody. Such an animal was not free in any admirable sense. It was a problem. The question at the head of this passage asks a listener whether he thinks he is one of those, and the picture would have arrived instantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah this passage closes opens with an oath by the self-reproaching soul, a phrase found nowhere else in the Quran. So the chapter runs from the part of a person that accuses itself to the question of whether that person was left unattended, and the two ends answer each other: something in you already keeps account.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs from origin to destination without a step in between, which is the passage's method. If a person began as something with no shape and was brought to a body in stages, then reassembly is not a larger task than assembly was. But the opening question is doing something else. It ties resurrection to purpose: being raised is presented not as a threat but as evidence that a life was being attended to.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same sequence of stages in more detail and ends by blessing the best of makers.
Puts the Meccan objection in a scene and answers it with the same argument from first making.
Asks the same question about purpose in almost the same words, and links it to being returned.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would do differently today if you were certain nobody was keeping any record of it. Then notice how much of your answer is about small things: how you speak to someone you will not see again, what you do with ten unwatched minutes. The ayah's question is about being attended to, and that is where it shows.
